title: A windowsill herb garden for small kitchens
description: Basil, mint and chives ask for little more than a pot, some compost and a bright sill, and they repay you at dinner.

body.heading: Why herbs suit beginners
paragraphs: Herbs are forgiving, fast and useful in quantities a windowsill can actually supply. A small bunch of fresh herbs from a shop often costs as much as a whole living plant, and the plant keeps giving for months.

Start with what you cook. Basil for tomato dishes, mint for teas and salads, chives for eggs and potatoes, parsley for almost everything. Two or three pots you truly use beat a jungle you admire and forget.

body.heading: Setting up in an afternoon
paragraphs: Supermarket living herbs are a cheap start, though they are often several crowded seedlings in one pot; splitting them gently into two or three pots with fresh compost helps them last far longer. Pots need drainage holes and a saucer to protect the sill.

Herbs want the brightest spot you have and watering when the surface feels dry, not on a fixed schedule. Turning the pots a quarter turn every few days keeps growth even instead of leaning toward the glass.

body.heading: Harvesting so plants keep giving
paragraphs: Pick little and often, taking the top growth of basil and mint, which encourages bushier plants, and snipping chives near the base. Never strip more than about a third of a plant at once.
If a herb races ahead of your cooking, chop the surplus into ice-cube trays with a little water or oil and freeze it. Future dinners will thank present you.

takeaway: Two or three pots of the herbs you cook with most will pay for themselves within weeks.
